title: Byzantine Anno Mundi Calendar
intro: This medieval Eastern Roman system numbers years from a traditional date for the creation of the world rather than from the Christian era. Each year begins on 1 September.
summary: Julian dates, a September New Year and Anno Mundi years.
epoch: 'Anno Mundi' means 'year of the world'. Its traditional starting point is 1 September 5509 BCE in the Julian framework, a religious chronology rather than a measured date of creation.
year_rule: The calendar runs through twelve Julian months but starts the new year in September. A date in the following August is still in the same Anno Mundi year.
after_note: Julian and today's Gregorian calendar do not always show the same day number. A historical Byzantine date needs its calendar specified.
history_heading: WHAT WAS THE ERA USED FOR?
history: Byzantine Christians developed this world-era reckoning for chronicles, religious and official dating. A September year boundary distinguished it from a January-start civil year. The year number describes a theological era convention, not a scientific estimate of Earth's age.
limits: The model follows the Constantinopolitan Anno Mundi convention. Historical records used related systems and variants; not every medieval source used exactly the same reckoning.
